drafts.retell: Larry walks you home past a laundromat nobody ever finishes, and at his door an old Tamil couplet about guests means he cannot leave you standing outside.
drafts.evidence: MOVES 4. The feeling is made by what happens at the door, not asked for: we stay on the pavement (cue listen-door), q-come-up, guest-1 and guest-2, 'So you see my position.' (position), the door buzzing open because someone upstairs saw him coming (cue buzzed-in), 'You're late. Nobody has started.' (late), 'I brought someone.' (brought), 'Chair.' (chair), a place sliding in (cue chair-in). No speech and no line tells the viewer how to feel. Down a point: there is a quip at nearly every stop (cold, wasnt-here, weekend, story, laundry, better-one, this-morning, sibyl-would, position), so the earnest register is left to rattled through cant-fix and the stretch from work-1 to assignment, and 'It's the whole assignment.' (assignment) sums the idea up. INTERESTING 4. The turn only this special has is an old couplet used as the reason he cannot go up alone. 'Nobody has ever finished the laundry.' and 'Somebody was always rattled first.' (old-books) would be quoted. TELEVISION 4. The best single pictures in the three drafts are here: pass-restaurant (one silhouette bobbing on its own, the others still, then all rocking) lands story; pass-laundromat's pile that is not getting smaller lands laundry; pass-scaffold puts the studio's own work lamp behind work-1 and work-2. Every cue is chest-up and hand-free and a builder could stage it. Against: twelve places and 38 cues with only 26 seconds of waits, the least room to look of the three; three small source lines sit on screen while he quotes (gutter-stream, pass-scaffold, listen-door), which is reading matter however small; a lid lifts itself at lid-off. LARRY 4. Dry, kind and never the expert: 'I've stretched it. I hope it's allowed.' (stretched), 'Somebody had already underlined it.' (used-book), 'As I remember it' (guest-1). The device sounds like talk: q-how after a held second, and the-look, where he answers a look and does not say it back. But he has a line for every shopfront, which is the host on the air, and the outline asks for a man less quick to joke. The crew are themselves (Sibyl rules twice, Al says one word, Hy speaks for Pete, Eppy calls eight at a table for six, Dee sings it), but one after another in twenty seconds: a roll call, as the writer's own worry says. IDEAS 3. Tarfon is clear, usable tonight and earned by the laundry joke before it. The Tirukkural couplet is used, not displayed. The Hojoki is displayed and its answer turned down (hut, weekend), so it offers nothing to use; it has the hardest sentence for the voice ('unceasingly') and, with tamil-book, two of the hardest names in any draft. Three cultures, and not a list, because each does a different job. No attribution looks wrong to me; stream-2 ends on a full stop the source does not have, as the writer notes.
wouldNotBeMissed: poet, opened, stream-1, stream-2, he-meant, hut (cue gutter-stream): the change it describes is already said and shown at pass-shutters (shoe-shop, wasnt-here), and its answer is turned down, so nothing is offered. Only weekend would be missed
the three source lines on screen at gutter-stream, pass-scaffold and listen-door: footnotes on a walk; the credits can name the translations
lid-off: a lid lifting by itself, after the room is already warm at chair-in
eppy-counts or dee-sings: the fifth and sixth greetings in twenty seconds, by which point it is a roll call
nothing-coming without sibyl-would: all three writers arrived at waiting for the light on an empty road; only the second line is this draft's
drafts.fixedPoints: ok. All five owner's lines in their places, 432 words, the viewer makes footsteps only, the holiday and its food unnamed, the last words the owner's. The table line is taken in two beats with the glance-back cue and a tick between them, which puts a sight gag inside the owner's sentence: the owner should see that.
drafts.reason: Read against both aired records and every aired line: nothing returns. It opens on a switched-off studio and a work lamp (the pilot opened on black with the lights coming up on a host being built; 002-2026-w47 on a pen plotter) and closes on the owner's lines at a table and a cut to black (the pilot: a key press and a collapsing picture; 002: a toast, the widest shot, long applause). Looked at and passed: the scarf that draws itself on (the pilot's tuxedo drew itself on at the top as a joke about the host being built; this is the staging read's answer to a puppet with no hands, done in silence, and all three drafts have it, so it is a matter for staging, where the read's other option is a cut to the collar); gold as his colour is the cast chapter's and carries no punch here; Eppy's 'house record' is his nature and not a line he has said; Dee's four notes to 'you two' are an aside and resolve nothing; the envelope's 'L. NX' is a name, not a handle. The three provenance labels are a primitive that 002 used often, which is a note for the scorecard. The goodnight is the owner's line and is not judged.

drafts.retell: Larry walks you home, tells you at a red light on an empty road that we don't have to finish it and don't get to quit, and upstairs the house rule is that there is always one extra chair.
drafts.evidence: MOVES 4. True and earned: 'I don't have a joke for that.' / 'I looked.' (no-joke, i-looked); the viewer's hardest question said back (q-put-right) and answered first with 'I don't know. I really don't.' (dont-know) before any book; five seconds of snow with no words (cue cross); 'House rule. There is always one extra chair.' (house-rule) and the camera taking the chair (cue sit). Nothing tells the viewer how to feel. Down a point: the street answers him on cue three times (window-dark, cook-slows, walk-sign) and by the third a viewer can see it coming; the light turning green on his reading is a swell in picture form, even with 'I didn't arrange that.' (didnt-arrange) to puncture it; and table-tune (three voices, a home note, 'a second of quiet in the room') is a small musical swell at the arrival. INTERESTING 4. 'Things speed up, and the cook slows down.' and the extra chair would be retold. TELEVISION 5. The most carefully directed of the three. A picture lands on the word each time: cook-slows at -0.5 on 'slows down'; the one lit window going dark at window-dark; the red of the sign on his face from asked-put-right to tarfon-close, then green. The only text on screen is OPEN, DON'T WALK and WALK. Every cue is stageable from the staging read, and the shots at the table hold four heads or fewer outside two short wides. LARRY 4. The man with the show switched off: no-joke, 'I'm probably saying that wrong.' (zhuangzi-name), 'Me, I'd have waited for a crowd.' (waited-for-crowd), dont-know. The device is natural: 'Good.' in scarf takes our yes, and the three q- lines are questions a person would ask. The crew are themselves: Sibyl not looking up (late), Eppy on eleven minutes, a band that cannot help playing, 'Sit. Eat.' Down a point: mostly-lights is a joke about the show before we have left it; it is not clear whom 'Fine. Tomorrow, then.' (tomorrow-then) answers; and the scene at the door leans on Larry's flat note (see the verdict). IDEAS 4. All three are things to do tonight and clear on one hearing: get up to the work of a human being (marcus-quote), slow down at the hard part (cook-hard-part, cook-gently), don't finish and don't quit (dont-finish, dont-quit), and the third is asked for by the viewer. Down a point: the same inner shape runs three times (who, the telling, the street answers, Larry's button: tomorrow-then, cook-keep, didnt-arrange), and 'One was a Roman emperor.' opens it like a list. No attribution looks wrong to me.
wouldNotBeMissed: marcus-who to tomorrow-then (cues windows, emperor-look, window-dark): the first of three old books and the only one that answers nothing we asked or saw; the cook and the rabbi carry the special without it
lights-off, mostly-lights: a joke about the show itself, in the place where the outline wants him off it
full-house: says what the picture is already showing
larry-hums, hy-flat: see the verdict; the door can open without them
the steam grate at walk-on: nothing meets it
drafts.fixedPoints: ok. All five owner's lines in their places and the last three beats are the owner's, the viewer makes footsteps only, the holiday and the dish unnamed. 415 words by the count, and Dee's seven sung syllables inside the music block are on top of that, as the writer says: 422, in range.
drafts.avoid: Larry singing or humming a note that comes out wrong, a band member's dry verdict on it, and the band then carrying the tune home.
drafts.reason: One item repeats: larry-hums, hy-flat and table-tune. The song that closed 002-2026-w47 ended on the host singing one unsure note that was not the one the chord wanted, the bandleader's dry line to him by name ('We can work with that.'), and the band bringing the music home; both gate reviewers judged that ending a repeat of the pilot's, the owner kept it on purpose, and the ledger lists it as having aired twice. Here Larry hums, his last note is a semitone under, Hy says 'Nearly, Larry. Flat, but nearly.' with every head turned to him, and the band sings the tune to its home note. One sentence covers both without naming a subject. That the band corrects him here where it changed key for him there is a new shape, not a turn. The rest of the draft is fresh. Noted, not blocked: a tune left one note short of home and brought home by the band also rhymes with that ending's chord that wanted one more note, and without Larry's note in it I would pass it; waited-for-crowd ('Me, I'd have...') is the host owning up to the lesser instinct beside someone who simply made the thing, which 002's interview did with the same two opening words ('Me, I just say...'), in character once, a habit the next time; mostly-lights is a joke about the show itself, of which the bible allows one. The scarf: as under writer-1. The goodnight is the owner's and is not judged.

drafts.retell: Larry walks you home past a busker who has been one line short of a song since the spring, lets an old poem say he is glad of the company, and at his table Dee sings the missing line.
drafts.evidence: MOVES 4. The truest beats in the three drafts are here and none of them is asked for. 'So. How have you been?' (how-have-you-been), 2.2 seconds, 'Yeah. Me too.' (yeah-me-too): we answer and he does not even say it back. 'I'm a guest in that sentence.' (guest). 'Does it help? Some nights.' (does-it-help). And this-block, norse, comrade-line, the cue glance and 'That's the poem talking. Mostly.' (poem-talking): he tells us he is glad we came by saying someone else's line and not looking at us, and the walk has earned it. The lightness is his, late and small (a-cue, my-house). No speech, no summing-up, no line telling the viewer how to feel. Down a point for the last half minute: the meal is untouched, the viewer ends on the step (cue goodnight), and the payoff depends on sung words (busker-3, saved-a-seat). INTERESTING 5. It is a story, not a tour: a question he cannot answer (supposed-to-do), a busker one line short (since-spring), the rabbi's sentence, 'A thing with no last line.' (no-last-line), and a table that has the line. Only this special could hold it and a viewer would retell it in the sentence above. TELEVISION 4. The street and the words meet: the doorman's nod on 'I decided he did' (cue doorman-nods), two silhouettes over one plate on 'dessert' (cue dessert), the song stopping (cue song-stops), the signal changing on 'cue' (cue crossing-walk), an empty pavement under this-block. Nothing is put on screen to read. Against: the cue quote holds one close-up for about twenty seconds, tarfon to guest, with the street stopped; the busker stretch is carried by sung lyric; the envelope lifts out of frame by itself. LARRY 5. The slowest to joke and the most personal: 'They'd mail it. I like the walk home.' (mail-it), 'I usually walk this block on my own.' (this-block), 'There's one I say to myself here.' (norse). Never the expert: 'I'll say it my way.' (gatekeeper-says), 'I can't tell if the gatekeeper meant it kindly. I decided he did.' (meant-kindly), guest. The device sounds like conversation: 'What do I do about it? I read.' (what-do-i-do). The crew are the best of the three because they talk to him and not past him: house-rule, 'It's my house.' (my-house), 'It's still the rule.' (still-the-rule); 'You took the long way.' (long-way); 'I counted you in twice.' (counted-in); and Eppy says his record is a guess ('I believe'). IDEAS 4. Tarfon gets the best use in any draft: finish-quit as his own, then handed to the viewer's own unfinished thing (no-last-line, what-youve-got). The Havamal line is done, not displayed. The three arrive three different ways, so it is not a list. Down a point: the Analects block has two names and two layers of who said what about whom (analects, gatekeeper-says) before gatekeeper, which is a knotty sentence for one hearing in this voice. For the auditor: comrade-line ends on a full stop where the card's line ends on a comma mid-sentence, and guest says 'study' where the card says the study and practice of Torah. Neither looks wrong to me.
wouldNotBeMissed: analects, gatekeeper-says, gatekeeper (cues lobby-ahead, doorman-nods): the heaviest attribution for the lightest idea, and dessert-anyway says 'anyway' better with a picture. meant-kindly is the one line of the block that would be missed
the bus (cue bus): a sweep and a reflection that nothing he says meets
no-fix: see the verdict; fast-lately and what-do-i-do join without it
same-worries: tells what dessert-anyway then shows
drafts.fixedPoints: ok. All five owner's lines in their places, with mail-it added after the paycheck line and before the ask; 434 words; the viewer is never heard, not even as footsteps; the holiday and its food unnamed; the last three beats are the owner's.
drafts.avoid: Larry excusing himself from having an answer by naming his job as host; and the particular scat syllable written for the busker's missing words (any other will do).
drafts.reason: Two small items repeat and the rest is fresh, the spine included. (1) no-fix, 'I don't have a fix. I host a talk show.': the song that closed 002-2026-w47 turned on 'I only host.', which is also the last line of the show account's bio, and that episode's record says in terms that a joke whose punch is that he is only a host has been made. One sentence covers both. (2) busker-3's 'doo doo doo', sung and shown as lyric: 'doo' was that song's hook, a card on the band's stand and the card propped on his desk in its last frame, and there too it stood in for having nothing more to offer. A viewer of last week would hear it. Looked at hard and passed: Dee's saved-a-seat completes a line, lands a held-back home note and says 'you' to the host just before the goodnight, which brushes three things the ledger lists as aired twice (music that takes the host in, a last sung line whose words change toward 'you', music and then the goodnight). I judge it a different mechanism: nothing stops for the host, he does not sing, no light changes, and what is completed is a street singer's song from two minutes earlier. It would become the aired ending if the room were dimmed or stilled for her, or if Larry sang. The reviewers at the script gate should look again once the ending is rewritten. what-youve-got is a second-person invitation one week after the show told the cluster it could point the show at things; here it is a remark between two people walking and promises nothing, so not a repeat, but the owner should know it is there, since the show's account answers nobody. Pete has only ever spoken in unison on air; a line of his own is new and allowed by the cast chapter. The gold chair marks the seat as Larry's by the cast chapter's rule and carries no punch. The scarf: as under writer-1. The goodnight is the owner's and is not judged.

why: It is the one draft that is a story and not a tour: a question he cannot answer, a busker one line short, the rabbi's sentence, and a table that has the line. Its Larry is the outline's man: slowest to joke, most personal, and the conversation device sounds most like talk, best where he asks how we have been and answers 'Yeah. Me too.' without saying our answer back. comrade-line to poem-talking is the truest beat in the three drafts and is the experiment working: earnest, in his own way, with nothing asked of the viewer. Its two repeats are one line and one syllable, where writer-2's sits inside its payoff. Writer-2 is close behind, with the better pictures and the better table, and writer-1 is the only draft clean at the gate and the funniest, but its Larry has a line for every window. Writer-3 is good enough to go forward, on condition that the last half minute goes back: it does not yet end where the outline ends.
sendBack: no-fix: stopped at the repetition gate; see avoid.
busker-3, and its lyric as shown: the wordless syllable is stopped at the repetition gate; see avoid. The tune, and where it stops, are not in question.

table-wide to goodnight: the outline ends on a large group of close friends sharing a meal, with us there. Here nothing is touched, nobody eats, Larry never sits, and the last picture is Larry in the doorway between us and the room with snow in front of him. The one empty chair is drawn in his colour, so the seat Dee saved is his and no place is ours, and it is not clear whom 'Sit.' (sit) is said to. A viewer can take the end as the door closing on them, which undoes what comrade-line earned a minute earlier.

dee-sings, that-song, sit: the last thing that happens before the owner's lines is a puzzle (how does she know the song?) and it is left open. The table is on screen for about twenty-five seconds and a third of that is spent on where a tune came from, at the moment the room should be the point. The notes' answer, that she walked the same street, is nowhere a viewer can see or hear it.

busker-1 to busker-3 and saved-a-seat: the spine rests on sung words, which the voice does least clearly. since-spring and that-song carry the sense if the lyric is lost, but then both the set-up and the payoff are told to the viewer and neither is heard. The writer's worry stands and nothing in the script yet answers it.

analects, gatekeeper-says, gatekeeper: two names and two layers of who said what about whom before the idea arrives, and gatekeeper is a knotty sentence for one hearing. It is the idea a viewer would not miss, and the brief asked for fewer if fewer land harder. Only meant-kindly earns its place.

cue quote, lines tarfon to guest: about twenty seconds on one held close-up with the street stopped. The words are the point, but this is the centre of the piece and the one stretch where the place does nothing while he talks.

supposed-to-do: the pivot question has no cue of its own. It follows dessert-anyway in the same shot, and 'you' can be heard as Larry thinking aloud. If a viewer does not take the question as theirs, the busker answers nobody.

what-youve-got: he asks to hear it, and the piece gives us no way to tell him. The cues at crossing-red and snow-starts do not say that the silence which follows is ours, so the offer is dropped as soon as it is made.

fromOthers.what: Gives the central quotation in a place that is doing something: an empty road, a red light on his face (cues asked-put-right, looks-at-red, tarfon-close, two-at-the-kerb), three framings, and the light changing only after his own reading of it (cue walk-sign), which he then shrugs off. The pick gives the same quotation on one held close-up.
An old idea that is a thing to do tonight, shown happening on the word (cue cook-slows). The pick's first idea is a description of a man, and nothing on the street does it.
The crew make a place for the viewer by a rule, and the camera takes it (cues they-look, chair, sit); Larry says the owner's lines from the seat beside us. The pick leaves us on the step.

An old idea used as the reason for something he does: he cannot go up and leave us outside, and somebody upstairs was watching for him (cue buzzed-in). The pick's door opens with no moment at which we are asked in.

The meal starts while we are there: we learn in four words that they waited, a place slides in for us (cue chair-in), the lid comes off (cue lid-off), and the room carries on behind him through the owner's lines (cue larry-to-us). In the pick the table is a picture behind a doorway.
He owns up to having nothing for the size of it, and gets the small laugh, without reaching for what he does for a living. It does the job of the pick's stopped line.
Says what a table of friends is for, as a joke about strangers in a window, two minutes before we reach his. The pick's restaurant is about carrying on and plants nothing for the table.

measure: Play the finished special once, with sound, to three people who have not read the script, and ask each what Larry told them and which moment stayed with them: it worked if at least two give the don't-have-to-finish, don't-get-to-quit idea in their own words, at least two name something that happens and not something they were told to feel, and none calls it a speech, a lesson or a list; and its cues hold no laugh, applause or sting.
